questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The current through the circular coil is halved and the radius of the coil is doubled. If $B_1$ and $B_2$ are respectively the initial and final magnetic field strength, then:
questions.solution:
The magnetic field at the center of a circular coil is given by $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$.

Initial magnetic field is $B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$.

The current is halved, so $I' = \dfrac{I}{2}$.

The radius is doubled, so $R' = 2R$.

Final magnetic field is $B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I'}{2R'} = \dfrac{\mu_0 \left(\dfrac{I}{2}\right)}{2(2R)} = \dfrac{1}{4} \left(\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}\right).$

Therefore, $B_2 = \dfrac{B_1}{4}.$

Answer: $B_2 = \dfrac{B_1}{4}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A circular coil of radius $r = 10\,cm$ having 300 turns carries a current of 2A. The coil is suspended vertically in a uniform magnetic field of strength 0.7 T. If the plane of the coil makes an angle $30^{}^{\circ}$ with the magnetic field, the torque needed to prevent it from turning is:
questions.solution:
Given:
Number of turns, $N = 300$
Current, $I = 2 \text{ A}$
Radius, $r = 10 \text{ cm} = 0.1 \text{ m}$
Magnetic field, $B = 0.7 \text{ T}$

The angle between the plane of the coil and the magnetic field is $30^{}^{\circ}$.
The angle between the area vector (normal to the plane) and the magnetic field is $\theta = 90^{}^{\circ} - 30^{}^{\circ} = 60^{}^{\circ}$.

Area of the coil, $A = \pi r^2 = \pi (0.1)^2 = 0.01\pi \text{ m}^2$

The torque experienced by the coil is given by:
$\tau = N I A B \sin\theta$

Substituting the values:
$\tau = 300 \times 2 \times 0.01\pi \times 0.7 \times \sin 60^{}^{\circ}$

$\tau = 6\pi \times 0.7 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

$\tau = 2.1 \pi \sqrt{3}$

Using $\pi \approx 3.14$ and $\sqrt{3} \approx$1.732$:
\tau \approx 2.1 \times 3.14 \times 1.732 \approx 11.42 \text{ Nm}$

The torque needed to prevent the coil from turning is equal in magnitude to the torque experienced by it, which is $11.42 \text{ Nm}$.

Answer: $11.42$ Nm

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two long parallel conductors X and Y are placed vertically at a distance d apart. Conductor X carries a current I upwards and conductor Y carries a current 2I downwards. A third long conductor Z is placed parallel to both X and Y and between X and Y. If Z carries a current I upwards and is at a distance $x$ from conductor X, then:
options: All the conductors are in equilibrium and the net force on Z is zero
The net force on Z is $\dfrac{\mu_0 I²}{2x\pi} \left[\dfrac{d+x}{d-x}\right]$towards X
The net force on Z is $\dfrac{\mu_0 I²}{2x\pi} \left[\dfrac{d+x}{d-x}\right]$towards Y
The net force on Z is $\dfrac{\mu_0 I²}{2x\pi} \left[\dfrac{d-x}{d+x}\right]$towards Y
questions.solution:
The force per unit length between two parallel current-carrying wires is given by $F = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi r}$.

Wires carrying current in the same direction attract each other, while wires carrying current in opposite directions repel each other.

The force per unit length on wire Z due to wire X is:
$F_{ZX} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I \cdot I}{2\pi x} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I^2}{2\pi x}$
Since the currents in X and Z are in the same direction (upwards), this force is attractive. Therefore, $F_{ZX}$ is directed towards X.

The force per unit length on wire Z due to wire Y is:
$F_{ZY} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I \cdot 2I}{2\pi (d-x)} = \dfrac{\mu_0 2I^2}{2\pi (d-x)}$
Since the currents in Y and Z are in opposite directions (Y is downwards, Z is upwards), this force is repulsive. Therefore, $F_{ZY}$ is directed away from Y, which is also towards X.

The net force per unit length on wire Z is the sum of these two forces, as they act in the same direction:
$F_{net} = F_{ZX} + F_{ZY}$

$F_{net} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I^2}{2\pi x} + \dfrac{\mu_0 2I^2}{2\pi (d-x)}$

$F_{net} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I^2}{2\pi} \left[ \dfrac{1}{x} + \dfrac{2}{d-x} \right]

$ F_{net} = $\dfrac{\mu_0 I^2}{2\pi} \left[ \dfrac{d - x + 2x}{x(d-x)} \right]<$ br>
$F_{net} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I²}{2\pi x} \left[ \dfrac{d+x}{d-x} \right]$

The direction of the net force is towards X.

Answer: The net force on Z is $\dfrac{\mu_0 I²}{2x\pi} \left[\dfrac{d+x}{d-x}\right]$ towards X

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A proton is moving along negative X axis. If a uniform magnetic field is applied parallel to the positive Z axis, then choose the correct answer from the following options;
1. The proton will experience magnetic force along positive Y direction and will move along a circular path in the XY plane
2. The proton will experience magnetic force along negative Y direction and will move along a circular path in the XY plane
3. The proton will experience magnetic force along positive Y direction and will move along a circular path in the XZ plane
4. The proton will experience magnetic force along negative Y direction and will move along a circular path in the XZ plane
questions.solution:
Velocity of the proton, $\vec{v} = -v \hat{i}$

Magnetic field, $\vec{B} = B \hat{k}$

Charge of the proton, $q = +e$

The magnetic force experienced by the proton is given by $\vec{F} = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$

Substituting the values, $\vec{F} = e(-v \hat{i} \times B \hat{k}) = -ev(\hat{i} \times \hat{k})$

Since $\hat{i} \times \hat{k} = -\hat{j}$, we get $\vec{F} = ev \hat{j}$

The magnetic force is along the positive Y direction.

Since the velocity and force both lie in the XY plane and the magnetic field is perpendicular to it, the proton will move along a circular path in the XY plane.

Answer: 1

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The magnetic field at the centre of a wire loop formed by two semicircular wires of radii $r_1$ = 3.14m and $r_2$ = 6.28m and carrying a current of I =2A is:
questions.solution:
The magnetic field at the centre of the loop is the vector sum of the magnetic fields produced by the four segments of the wire: two straight segments and two semicircular arcs.

For the straight segments, the line of action of the current passes through the centre of the loop. Therefore, the angle between the current element $d\vec{l}$ and the position vector $\vec{r}$ is $0$ or $\pi$. The magnetic field due to these segments at the centre is zero.

For the semicircular arcs, the magnetic field at the centre is given by $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4r}$.

The current in the larger semicircle of radius $r_2$ flows in the counter-clockwise direction. By the right-hand thumb rule, its magnetic field at the centre is directed outwards (out of the page).
$B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4r_2}$

The current in the smaller semicircle of radius $r_1$ also flows in the counter-clockwise direction. Its magnetic field at the centre is also directed outwards.
$B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4r_1}$

Since both magnetic fields are in the same direction, the net magnetic field at the centre is their sum:
$B_{\text{net}} = B_1 + B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4} \left( \dfrac{1}{r_1} + \dfrac{1}{r_2} \right)

Given:
$ I = 2$\text{ A}
$ r_1 = 3.14$\text{ m} \approx \pi\text{ m}
$ r_2 = 6.28$\text{ m} \approx2\pi\text{ m}
$\mu_0 = 4$\pi \times10^{-7}\text{ T}\cdot\text{m/A}

Substituting the values:
$ B_{$\text{net}$} = $\dfrac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 2}{4} \left( \dfrac{1}{\pi} + \dfrac{1}{2\pi} \right)

B_{\text{net}$} = $2\pi \times10^{-7} \left( \dfrac{2 + 1}{2\pi} \right)$

$B_{\text{net}} = 2\pi \times10^{-7} \left( \dfrac{3}{2\pi} \right)

B_{\text{net}$} = 3 $\times10^{-7}\text{ T}

Answer: 3 \times10^{-7}\ T$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
In the arrangement shown below, what is the magnitude of force experienced by 20 cm length of wire $Z$
Distance between the wires $X$ and $Z$ is 9 cm and between $X$ and $Y$ is 6 cm.
questions.solution:
The magnetic field $B$ at a distance $r$ from a long straight wire carrying current $I$ is given by $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 \pi r}$. The force per unit length between two parallel wires carrying currents $I_1$ and $I_2$ separated by distance $r$ is $f = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2 \pi r}$.

Let the wires be $X, Y, Z$ with currents $I_X = 45 A$, $I_Y = 15 A$, and $I_Z = 20 A$.
The distance between $X$ and $Z$ is $r_{XZ} = 9 cm = 0.09 m$.
The distance between $Y$ and $Z$ is $r_{YZ} = r_{XZ} - r_{XY} = 9 cm - 6 cm = 3 cm = 0.03 m$.

The magnetic field at wire $Z$ due to wire $X$ is $B_X = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_X}{2 \pi r_{XZ}}$. The force per unit length on $Z$ due to $X$ is $f_{ZX} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_X I_Z}{2 \pi r_{XZ}}$.
Substituting values: $f_{ZX} = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 45 \times 20}{0.09} = \dfrac{1800 \times 10^{-7}}{0.09} = 2 \times 10^{-3} N/m$. Since $I_X$ and $I_Z$ are in opposite directions (up and down), the force is repulsive.

The magnetic field at wire $Z$ due to wire $Y$ is $B_Y = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_Y}{2 \pi r_{YZ}}$. The force per unit length on $Z$ due to $Y$ is $f_{ZY} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_Y I_Z}{2 \pi r_{YZ}}$.
Substituting values: $f_{ZY} = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 15 \times 20}{0.03} = \dfrac{600 \times 10^{-7}}{0.03} = 2 \times 10^{-3} N/m$. Since $I_Y$ and $I_Z$ are in opposite directions, the force is repulsive.

Both forces $f_{ZX}$ and $f_{ZY}$ act in the same direction (away from $X$ and $Y$). The net force per unit length is $f_{net} = f_{ZX} + f_{ZY} = 2 \times 10^{-3} + 2 \times 10^{-3} = 4 \times 10^{-3} N/m$.

For a length $L = 20 cm = 0.2 m$, the total force is $F = f_{net} \times L = 4 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.2 = 0.8 \times 10^{-3} N = 8 \times 10^{-4} N$.

Answer: $8 \times 10^{-4} N$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A bar magnet is suspended in a uniform magnetic field of field strength 0.36 T. If the magnetic moment of the bar magnet is $4 \mathrm{Am}^2$ then the work done in rotating the magnet from its most stable position to its most unstable position is:
questions.solution:
The potential energy $U$ of a magnetic dipole with magnetic moment $\vec{M}$ in a uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$ is given by $U = -\vec{M} \cdot \vec{B} = -MB \cos \theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{M}$ and $\vec{B}$.

The most stable position corresponds to $\theta = 0^{{}^{\circ}}$, where $U_{initial} = -MB \cos(0^{{}^{\circ}}) = -MB$.

The most unstable position corresponds to $\theta = 180^{{}^{\circ}}$, where $U_{final} = -MB \cos(180^{{}^{\circ}}) = MB$.

The work done $W$ in rotating the magnet is the change in potential energy: $W = U_{final} - U_{initial} = MB - (-MB) = 2MB$.

Given $M = 4 \text{ Am}^2$ and $B = 0.36 \text{ T}$, we have $W = 2 \times 4 \times 0.36 = 8 \times 0.36 = 2.88 \text{ J}$.

Answer: 2.88 J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A straight wire carrying current of 21 A is bent into an arc of radius 11 cm as shown below. The magnetic field produced by the current at the centre $O$ of the arc is:
questions.solution:
The straight segments pass through centre $O$, so they produce no magnetic field at $O$.

The arc is a quarter circle, so $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r} \cdot \theta = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r} \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{2} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{8r}$

$B = \dfrac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 21}{8 \times 0.11} = \dfrac{4 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 3 \times 10^{-7}}{0.88} = \dfrac{264 \times 10^{-7}}{0.88}$

$B = 300 \times 10^{-7} = 0.3 \times 10^{-4}$ T

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A long solenoid X having 400 turns per cm carries a current I . The magnetic field produced at its centre by this solenoid is $3.14 \times 10^{-2} T$. The magnetic field produced by another solenoid $Y$ at its centre having 300 turns per cm carries a current $\dfrac{\mathrm{I}}{3}$. The magnetic field produced by Y at its centre is:
questions.solution:
The magnetic field $B$ at the centre of a long solenoid is given by the formula $B = \mu_{0} n I$, where $n$ is the number of turns per unit length and $I$ is the current.

For solenoid X, we have $n_{X} = 400 \text{ turns/cm} = 40000 \text{ turns/m}$ and $B_{X} = 3.14 \times 10^{-2} \text{ T}$.

For solenoid Y, we have $n_{Y} = 300 \text{ turns/cm} = 30000 \text{ turns/m}$ and current $I_{Y} = \dfrac{I}{3}$.

Taking the ratio of the magnetic fields:

$\dfrac{B_{Y}}{B_{X}} = \dfrac{\mu_{0} n_{Y} I_{Y}}{\mu_{0} n_{X} I_{X}} = \dfrac{n_{Y}}{n_{X}} \times \dfrac{I_{Y}}{I_{X}}$

Substituting the values:

$\dfrac{B_{Y}}{3.14 \times 10^{-2}} = \dfrac{300}{400} \times \dfrac{I/3}{I} = \dfrac{3}{4} \times \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{1}{4}$

$B_{Y} = \dfrac{3.14 \times 10^{-2}}{4} \text{ T} = 0.785 \times 10^{-2} \text{ T}$.

Answer: $0.785 \times 10^{-2} T$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Which physical quantity has the unit joule / tesla?
questions.solution:
The energy $U$ of a magnetic dipole in an external magnetic field $B$ is given by the relation $U = -\vec{m} \cdot \vec{B}$, where $m$ is the magnetic dipole moment and $B$ is the magnetic induction.

Rearranging this equation for the magnetic dipole moment $m$, we get $m = \dfrac{U}{B}$.

The unit of energy $U$ is Joule (J) and the unit of magnetic induction $B$ is Tesla (T).

Therefore, the unit of magnetic dipole moment $m$ is Joule per Tesla (J/T).

Answer: Magnetic dipole moment

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A rectangular coil of length 10 cm and breadth 9 cm carries a current of 10 A. A long straight conductor carrying a current of 20 A is placed 1 cm from the coil parallel to its length and in the same plane of the coil. What will be the net force acting on the straight conductor?
questions.solution:
Forces on the breadth arms cancel. Net force is the difference between forces on the two length arms ($L = 0.1$ m).

Force formula: $F = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2 L}{2\pi r}$

Nearer arm at $r_1 = 1$ cm $= 0.01$ m:
$F_1 = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 20 \times 10 \times 0.1}{0.01} = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 200 \times 0.1}{0.01} = 4 \times 10^{-4}$ N

Farther arm at $r_2 = 1 + 9 = 10$ cm $= 0.1$ m:
$F_2 = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 20 \times 10 \times 0.1}{0.1} = 0.4 \times 10^{-4}$ N

$F_{net} = F_1 - F_2 = 4 \times 10^{-4} - 0.4 \times 10^{-4} = 3.6 \times 10^{-4}$ N

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The wire made of Phosphor bronze is used as the suspension strip in the moving coil galvanometer, because:
options: Its restoring torque per unit twist is very large
Its restoring torque per unit twist is small.
questions.solution:
The moving coil galvanometer operates on the principle of balancing the magnetic deflecting torque with the restoring torque of the suspension strip.

The deflecting torque is given by $\tau_{d} = NIAB \sin \theta$, where $N$ is the number of turns, $I$ is the current, $A$ is the area, and $B$ is the magnetic field.

The restoring torque is given by $\tau_{r} = k \theta$, where $k$ is the restoring torque per unit twist of the suspension strip.

For a sensitive galvanometer, a small current $I$ should produce a large deflection $\theta$. Since $\theta = \dfrac{NIAB}{k}$, a small value of $k$ is required to achieve high sensitivity.

Phosphor bronze is chosen for the suspension strip because it has a very small restoring torque per unit twist, which allows the galvanometer to detect very small currents.

Answer: Its restoring torque per unit twist is small.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In to a uniform transverse magnetic field, two charged particles having the same mass and charge enter and move in two different circular paths. The ratio of the radii of curvatures of the circular paths is $1: 4$. What would be the ratio of their respective velocities?
questions.solution:
The radius $r$ of the circular path of a charged particle moving in a uniform transverse magnetic field $B$ is given by the formula $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$, where $m$ is the mass, $v$ is the velocity, and $q$ is the charge of the particle.

Given that the mass $m$ and charge $q$ are the same for both particles, and the magnetic field $B$ is uniform, the radius $r$ is directly proportional to the velocity $v$. That is, $r \propto v$.

Therefore, the ratio of the radii of the two circular paths is equal to the ratio of their respective velocities:

$\dfrac{r_1}{r_2} = \dfrac{v_1}{v_2}$

Given that the ratio of the radii is $1: 4$, we have:

$\dfrac{v_1}{v_2} = \dfrac{r_1}{r_2} = \dfrac{1}{4}$

Thus, the ratio of their respective velocities is $1: 4$.

Answer: $\dfrac{r_1}{r_2}=1: 4$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a particular case $X$, a certain length of insulated copper wire is bent to form double loops of equal radii. In another case Y the same copper wire is bent to form three loops of equal radii. If the same steady current is passed through the copper wire in both the cases, the ratio of magnetic field at the centre in the case X to that in case Y is:
questions.solution:
Let $L$ be the total length of the wire. In case $X$, the wire is bent into $n_1 = 2$ loops of radius $r_1$. The circumference of these loops is $2 \times (2 \pi r_1) = L$, so $r_1 = \dfrac{L}{4 \pi}$.

The magnetic field at the center of $n_1$ loops is $B_X = n_1 \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 r_1} = 2 \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 (L / 4 \pi)} = \dfrac{4 \pi \mu_0 I}{L}$.

In case $Y$, the wire is bent into $n_2 = 3$ loops of radius $r_2$. The circumference of these loops is $3 \times (2 \pi r_2) = L$, so $r_2 = \dfrac{L}{6 \pi}$.

The magnetic field at the center of $n_2$ loops is $B_Y = n_2 \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 r_2} = 3 \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 (L / 6 \pi)} = \dfrac{9 \pi \mu_0 I}{L}$.

The ratio of the magnetic fields is $\dfrac{B_X}{B_Y} = \dfrac{4 \pi \mu_0 I / L}{9 \pi \mu_0 I / L} = \dfrac{4}{9}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{4}{9}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A current carrying closed loop in the form of a right isosceles triangle XYZ is placed in a uniform magnetic field $B$ acting along $X Y$ of the loop. If the magnetic force on the $\operatorname{arm} Y Z$ is $\sqrt{2}$F$, then the force on the arm $X Z$ is:
$
questions.solution:
The net magnetic force on a closed current-carrying loop in a uniform field is zero:
$\vec{F}_{XY} + \vec{F}_{YZ} + \vec{F}_{XZ} = 0$

Since field $B$ acts along arm $XY$, the arm $XY$ is parallel to $\vec{B}$, so $\vec{F}_{XY} = 0$.

Therefore:
$\vec{F}_{XZ} = -\vec{F}_{YZ} = -\sqrt{2}F$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A short bar magnet placed with its axis at $45^{{}^{\circ}}$ with an external field of $400 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{ T}$ experiences a torque of 0.024 Nm. If a solenoid of cross-sectional area $10^{-4} \mathrm{ m}^2$ and 500 turns replaces the short bar magnet such that they have the same magnetic moment, then the current flowing through the solenoid is:
questions.solution:
The torque $\tau$ experienced by a magnetic dipole in an external magnetic field $B$ is given by $\tau = mB \sin \theta$, where $m$ is the magnetic moment and $\theta$ is the angle between the magnetic moment and the magnetic field.

Given $\tau = 0.024 \text{ Nm}$, $B = 400 \times 10^{-4} \text{ T} = 0.04 \text{ T}$, and $\theta = 45^{{}^{\circ}}$.

Substituting the values: $0.024 = m \times 0.04 \times \sin(45^{{}^{\circ}})$.

$0.024 = m \times 0.04 \times \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$.

$m = \dfrac{0.024 \times \sqrt{2}}{0.04} = 0.6 \sqrt{2} \text{ Am}^2$.

The magnetic moment of a solenoid is given by $m = NIA$, where $N$ is the number of turns, $I$ is the current, and $A$ is the cross-sectional area.

Given $N = 500$ and $A = 10^{-4} \text{ m}^2$.

Equating the magnetic moments: $0.6 \sqrt{2} = 500 \times I \times 10^{-4}$.

$0.6 \sqrt{2} = 0.05 \times I$.

$I = \dfrac{0.6 \sqrt{2}}{0.05} = \dfrac{60 \sqrt{2}}{5} = 12 \sqrt{2} \text{ A}$.

Answer: $12 \sqrt{2} \mathrm{ A}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A straight wire of mass 250 g and length 2.5 m carries a current of 4 A. It can be suspended in mid air by a uniform horizontal magnetic field of magnitude:
questions.solution:
The wire is suspended in mid-air, which implies that the magnetic force acting on the wire must balance the gravitational force acting on it.

The gravitational force $F_g$ acting on the wire is given by $F_g = mg$, where $m = 250 \text{ g} = 0.25 \text{ kg}$ and $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$.

$F_g = 0.25 \times 9.8 = 2.45 \text{ N}$.

The magnetic force $F_m$ on a current-carrying wire in a uniform magnetic field is given by $F_m = IlB \sin(\theta)$. Since the magnetic field is horizontal and the wire is suspended, the force is perpendicular to the wire, so $\theta = 90^{{}^{\circ}}$ and $\sin(90^{{}^{\circ}}) = 1$.

$F_m = IlB$.

Equating the forces, $IlB = mg$.

$B = \dfrac{mg}{Il} = \dfrac{0.25 \times 9.8}{4 \times 2.5} = \dfrac{2.45}{10} = 0.245 \text{ T}$.

Answer: 0.245 T

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A current loop consists of two identical semicircular parts each of radius $2 R$, one lying in the $x-y$ plane and the other in $x-z$ plane. If the current in the loop is $I$, the resultant magnetic field due to two semicircular parts at their common centre is
questions.solution:
The magnetic field at the center of a semicircular loop of radius $r$ carrying current $I$ is given by $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4r}$.

In this problem, the radius of each semicircular part is $2R$. Therefore, the magnitude of the magnetic field due to each semicircular part at the common center is $B_1 = B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4(2R)} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{8R}$.

The first semicircular part lies in the $x-y$ plane. By the right-hand rule, its magnetic field vector is directed along the $z$-axis, so $\vec{B}_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{8R} \hat{k}$.

The second semicircular part lies in the $x-z$ plane. By the right-hand rule, its magnetic field vector is directed along the $y$-axis, so $\vec{B}_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{8R} \hat{j}$.

Since the two magnetic field vectors are perpendicular to each other, the resultant magnetic field magnitude is $B_{net} = \sqrt{B_1^2 + B_2^2} = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{8R}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{8R}\right)^2}$.

$B_{net} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{8R} \sqrt{1^2 + 1^2} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{8R} \sqrt{2} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4 \sqrt{2} R}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{\mu_o I}{4 \sqrt{2} R}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A charged particle is released from rest in a region of space in which steady and uniform electric and magnetic fields are parallel to each other. The particle will move in a
questions.solution:
The force on a charged particle moving in electric and magnetic fields is given by the Lorentz force equation: $\vec{F} = q(\vec{E} + \vec{v} \times \vec{B})$.

Given that the electric field $\vec{E}$ and magnetic field $\vec{B}$ are parallel, let $\vec{E} = E\hat{k}$ and $\vec{B} = B\hat{k}$. The particle is released from rest, so its initial velocity $\vec{v} = 0$.

The initial force acting on the particle is $\vec{F} = q\vec{E} = qE\hat{k}$. This force causes the particle to accelerate in the direction of the electric field, which is along the $\hat{k}$ axis.

As the particle gains velocity $\vec{v}$ in the $\hat{k}$ direction, the magnetic force $\vec{F}_m = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$ is calculated. Since $\vec{v}$ is parallel to $\vec{B}$, the cross product $\vec{v} \times \vec{B} = 0$.

Consequently, the magnetic force remains zero throughout the motion. The particle continues to experience only the electric force $qE$ in the direction of the electric field. Since the initial velocity is zero and the net force is always parallel to the initial displacement, the particle moves in a straight line.

Answer: Straight line

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two very long, straight, parallel wires carry steady currents I and 2I respectively. The distance between the wires is d. At a certain instant of time, a point charge q is at a point equidistant from the two wires, in the plane of the wires. Its instantaneous velocity is v perpendicular to this plane. The magnitude of the force due to the magnetic field acting on the charge at this instant is
questions.solution:
The magnetic field due to both wires at any point in the plane of the wires is perpendicular to that plane.

The velocity $v$ of charge $q$ is also perpendicular to the plane of the wires.

Since $\vec{v}$ and $\vec{B}$ are both perpendicular to the same plane, they are collinear (parallel or anti-parallel), so $\theta = 0°$ or $180°$.

$F = qvB\sin\theta = qvB \times 0 = 0$

questions.q: A circular ring of radius $r$ is placed in a homogeneous magnetic field perpendicular to the plane of the ring. The field $B$ changes with time according to the equation $B=K t$, where $K$ is a constant and $t$ is the time. The electric field in the ring is

questions.q: A long horizontal wire $\mathrm{P}$ carries current of $50 \mathrm{ A}$ from left to right. It is rigidly fixed. Another fine wire $\mathrm{Q}$ is placed directly above and parallel to $\mathrm{P}$. The mass of the wire is '$\mathrm{m}$' $\mathrm{kg}$ and carries a current of '$\mathrm{I}$' A. The direction of current in $\mathrm{Q}$ and position of wire $\mathrm{Q}$ from $\mathrm{P}$ so that the wire $\mathrm{Q}$ remains suspended are
options: $\text{ Right to left, } \quad \dfrac{25 I \mu_0}{\pi m g}$
$\text{ Right to left, } \quad \dfrac{50 I \mu_0}{\pi m g}$
$\text{ Left to right, } \quad \dfrac{25 I \mu_0}{\pi m g}$
questions.solution:
For the wire Q to remain suspended, the magnetic force acting on it must balance the gravitational force acting downwards. The magnetic force per unit length between two parallel wires carrying currents $I_1$ and $I_2$ separated by a distance $r$ is given by $F/L = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2 \pi r}$.

Since the wire Q is suspended above wire P, the magnetic force must be directed upwards (repulsive). For the force to be repulsive, the currents in the two parallel wires must flow in opposite directions. Given that wire P carries current from left to right, wire Q must carry current from right to left.

Equating the magnetic force to the weight per unit length of wire Q, we have $F/L = mg/L$. However, the problem implies the total force balances the total weight $mg$. Assuming the length of the wire is $L$, the force is $F = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2 L}{2 \pi r} = mg$.

Substituting $I_1 = 50 \text{ A}$ and $I_2 = I \text{ A}$, we get $\dfrac{\mu_0 (50) I L}{2 \pi r} = mg$.

Solving for $r$, we get $r = \dfrac{50 I \mu_0 L}{2 \pi mg} = \dfrac{25 I \mu_0 L}{\pi mg}$. Assuming the mass $m$ is given per unit length or the force balance is per unit length, the distance $r$ is $\dfrac{25 I \mu_0}{\pi mg}$.

Answer: $\text{ Right to left, } \quad \dfrac{25 I \mu_0}{\pi m g}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: To increase the current sensitivity of a moving coil galvanometer by $25 \%$, its resistance is increased so that the new resistance becomes twice its initial resistance. By what factor does the voltage sensitivity change?
questions.solution:
The current sensitivity of a moving coil galvanometer is given by $I_s = \dfrac{\theta}{I} = \dfrac{NAB}{k}$, where $N$ is the number of turns, $A$ is the area, $B$ is the magnetic field, and $k$ is the torsional constant of the spring.

The voltage sensitivity is given by $V_s = \dfrac{\theta}{V} = \dfrac{\theta}{IR} = \dfrac{I_s}{R}$, where $R$ is the resistance of the galvanometer.

Let the initial current sensitivity be $I_{s1}$ and initial resistance be $R_1$. The initial voltage sensitivity is $V_{s1} = \dfrac{I_{s1}}{R_1}$.

The new current sensitivity is $I_{s2} = I_{s1} + 0.25 I_{s1} = 1.25 I_{s1} = \dfrac{5}{4} I_{s1}$.

The new resistance is $R_2 = 2 R_1$.

The new voltage sensitivity is $V_{s2} = \dfrac{I_{s2}}{R_2} = \dfrac{1.25 I_{s1}}{2 R_1} = 0.625 \dfrac{I_{s1}}{R_1} = 0.625 V_{s1}$.

The change in voltage sensitivity is $V_{s2} - V_{s1} = 0.625 V_{s1} - V_{s1} = -0.375 V_{s1}$.

The percentage change is $-0.375 \times 100 \% = -37.5 \%$.

The negative sign indicates a decrease of $37.5 \%$.

Answer: Decreases by $37.5 \%$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A negative charge particle is moving upward in a magnetic field which is towards north. The particle is deflected towards
questions.solution:
The force on a moving charge in a magnetic field is given by the Lorentz force formula $\vec{F} = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$.

Here, the charge $q$ is negative. The velocity vector $\vec{v}$ is directed upward (along the positive z-axis, $\hat{k}$), and the magnetic field $\vec{B}$ is directed towards the north (along the positive y-axis, $\hat{j}$).

The cross product $\vec{v} \times \vec{B}$ is $\hat{k} \times \hat{j} = -\hat{i}$, which points towards the west.

Since the charge $q$ is negative, the force $\vec{F} = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$ will be in the direction opposite to $\vec{v} \times \vec{B}$.

Therefore, the force is directed towards the east.

Answer: East

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A wire of length $2 \mathrm{ m}$ carries a current of $1 \mathrm{ A}$ along the $\mathrm{x}$ axis. A magnetic field $B=B_0(i+j+k)$ tesla exists in space.
The magnitude of magnetic force on the wire is
questions.solution:
The magnetic force on a current-carrying wire is given by the formula $\vec{F} = I(\vec{L} \times \vec{B})$.

The length vector $\vec{L}$ of the wire is $2\hat{i}$ m, as it lies along the x-axis and has a length of $2$ m. The current $I$ is $1$ A.

The magnetic field is given as $\vec{B} = B_0(\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k})$.

Substituting these values into the force equation:
$\vec{F} = 1 \times (2\hat{i}) \times B_0(\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k})$
$\vec{F} = 2B_0 [(\hat{i} \times \hat{i}) + (\hat{i} \times \hat{j}) + (\hat{i} \times \hat{k})]$

Using the cross product properties $\hat{i} \times \hat{i} = 0$, $\hat{i} \times \hat{j} = \hat{k}$, and $\hat{i} \times \hat{k} = -\hat{j}$:
$\vec{F} = 2B_0 [0 + \hat{k} - \hat{j}] = 2B_0(\hat{k} - \hat{j})$

The magnitude of the force is $|\vec{F}| = |2B_0| \sqrt{(1)^2 + (-1)^2} = 2B_0 \sqrt{2}$.

Answer: 2$\sqrt2$ B_0$ N$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A current I flows in an infinitely long wire with cross section in the form of semi-circular ring of radius $1 \mathrm{ m}$. The magnitude of the magnetic induction along its axis is
questions.solution:
Current per unit angle: $dI = \dfrac{I}{\pi}d\theta$

Magnetic field due to element (infinite wire) at axis (distance $R$):

$dB = \dfrac{\mu_0 dI}{2\pi R} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi^2 R}d\theta$

By symmetry, only sine components add up:

$B_{net} = \int_0^{\pi} dB\sin\theta = \int_0^{\pi} \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi^2 R}\sin\theta \, d\theta$

$= \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi^2 R}[-\cos\theta]_0^{\pi}$

$= \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi^2 R}[1+1] = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{\pi^2 R}$

For $R = 1$ m:

$B_{net} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{\pi^2}$ T

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two circular coils of radius '$a$' and '$2 a$' are placed coaxially at a distance ' $x$ and '$2 x$' respectively from the origin along the $\mathrm{X}$-axis. If their planes are parallel to each other and perpendicular to the $\mathrm{X}$ - axis and both carry the same current in the same direction, then the ratio of the magnetic field induction at the origin due to the smaller coil to that of the bigger one is:
questions.solution:
The magnetic field $B$ at a distance $d$ along the axis of a circular coil of radius $R$ carrying current $I$ is given by the formula $B = \dfrac{\mu_{0} I R^{2}}{2(R^{2} + d^{2})^{3/2}}$.

For the smaller coil, the radius is $R_{1} = a$ and the distance from the origin is $d_{1} = x$. The magnetic field at the origin is $B_{1} = \dfrac{\mu_{0} I a^{2}}{2(a^{2} + x^{2})^{3/2}}$.

For the bigger coil, the radius is $R_{2} = 2a$ and the distance from the origin is $d_{2} = 2x$. The magnetic field at the origin is $B_{2} = \dfrac{\mu_{0} I (2a)^{2}}{2((2a)^{2} + (2x)^{2})^{3/2}}$.

Simplifying $B_{2}$: $B_{2} = \dfrac{\mu_{0} I (4a^{2})}{2(4a^{2} + 4x^{2})^{3/2}} = \dfrac{\mu_{0} I (4a^{2})}{2 \times 4^{3/2} (a^{2} + x^{2})^{3/2}} = \dfrac{\mu_{0} I (4a^{2})}{2 \times 8 (a^{2} + x^{2})^{3/2}} = \dfrac{\mu_{0} I a^{2}}{4 (a^{2} + x^{2})^{3/2}}$.

The ratio of the magnetic field of the smaller coil to the bigger coil is $\dfrac{B_{1}}{B_{2}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{\mu_{0} I a^{2}}{2(a^{2} + x^{2})^{3/2}}}{\dfrac{\mu_{0} I a^{2}}{4(a^{2} + x^{2})^{3/2}}} = \dfrac{4}{2} = 2:1$.

Answer: 2 : 1

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Current flows through uniform, square frames and their connecting wires as shown in the figure. In which case is the net magnetic field at the centre of the frame not zero?
questions.solution:
The square frame itself always produces zero net field at the centre (symmetric current paths cancel).

Cases A and B: External wires are directed radially (along diagonals) toward/away from the centre $\Rightarrow$ their line of action passes through the centre, so they produce zero field there.

Case D: Incoming and outgoing external wires are on opposite sides and symmetric $\Rightarrow$ their fields cancel at the centre.

Case C: Both external wires are collinear with the top edge and carry current in the same direction (left to right). By the right-hand rule, both produce fields pointing into the page at the centre — they add up instead of cancelling.

Net magnetic field at the centre is non-zero only in Case C.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A circular coil of radius $0.1 \mathrm{ m}$ is placed in the $\mathrm{X}-\mathrm{Y}$ plane and a current $2 \mathrm{ A}$ is passed through the coil in the clockwise direction when looking from above. Find the magnetic dipole moment of the current loop
questions.solution:
The magnetic dipole moment $\vec{m}$ of a current loop is given by the formula $\vec{m} = I \vec{A}$, where $I$ is the current and $\vec{A}$ is the area vector.

The radius of the coil is $r = 0.1 \text{ m}$. The area of the circular coil is $A = \pi r^2 = \pi (0.1)^2 = 0.01 \pi \text{ m}^2$.

The current $I = 2 \text{ A}$. The magnitude of the magnetic dipole moment is $m = I A = 2 \times 0.01 \pi = 0.02 \pi \text{ Am}^2$.

The coil is placed in the X-Y plane. According to the right-hand rule, for a clockwise current when viewed from above (looking down the positive Z-axis), the direction of the area vector $\vec{A}$ is along the negative Z-axis. Therefore, the magnetic dipole moment $\vec{m}$ is directed in the negative Z-direction.

Answer: $0.02 \pi \mathrm{Am}^2 \text{ in the }-\mathrm{ve} \mathrm{ Z}-\text{ direction }$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two similar coils $A$ and $B$ of radius '$r$' and number of turns '$N$' each are placed concentrically with their planes perpendicular to each other. If I and $2 \mathrm{I}$ are the respective currents passing through the coils then the net magnetic induction at the centre of the coils will be:
questions.solution:
The magnetic field at the center of a circular coil of radius $r$ with $N$ turns carrying current $I$ is given by $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 NI}{2r}$.

For coil $A$ with current $I$, the magnetic field is $B_A = \dfrac{\mu_0 NI}{2r}$.

For coil $B$ with current $2I$, the magnetic field is $B_B = \dfrac{\mu_0 N(2I)}{2r} = \dfrac{2\mu_0 NI}{2r} = \dfrac{\mu_0 NI}{r}$.

Since the planes of the coils are perpendicular to each other, the magnetic field vectors $\vec{B}_A$ and $\vec{B}_B$ are perpendicular to each other.

The net magnetic induction $B_{net}$ is given by the vector sum $B_{net} = \sqrt{B_A^2 + B_B^2}$.

$B_{net} = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\mu_0 NI}{2r}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{2\mu_0 NI}{2r}\right)^2}$

$B_{net} = \dfrac{\mu_0 NI}{2r} \sqrt{1^2 + 2^2}$

$B_{net} = \sqrt{5} \left(\dfrac{\mu_0 NI}{2r}\right)$

Answer: $\sqrt{5}\left(\mu_0 \dfrac{\mathrm{NI}}{2 \mathrm{r}}\right)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The radius of the current carrying circular coil is doubled keeping the current passing through it the same. Then the ratio of the magnetic field produced at the centre of the coil before the doubling of the radius to the magnetic field after doubling of the radius.
questions.solution:
The magnetic field $B$ at the centre of a circular coil of radius $R$ carrying current $I$ is given by the formula $B = \dfrac{\mu_{0} I}{2R}$.

Let the initial radius be $R_{1} = R$ and the initial magnetic field be $B_{1} = \dfrac{\mu_{0} I}{2R}$.

After doubling the radius, the new radius is $R_{2} = 2R$. The current $I$ remains the same. The new magnetic field is $B_{2} = \dfrac{\mu_{0} I}{2R_{2}} = \dfrac{\mu_{0} I}{2(2R)} = \dfrac{\mu_{0} I}{4R}$.

The ratio of the magnetic field before doubling to the magnetic field after doubling is $\dfrac{B_{1}}{B_{2}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{\mu_{0} I}{2R}}{\dfrac{\mu_{0} I}{4R}} = \dfrac{4R}{2R} = \dfrac{2}{1}$.

Therefore, the ratio is $2 : 1$.

Answer: 2 : 1

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A circular loop of area $0.04 \mathrm{ m}^2$ carrying a current of $10 \mathrm{ A}$ is held with its plane perpendicular to a magnetic field induction $0.4 \mathrm{ T}$ Then the torque acting on the circular loop is :
questions.solution:
The torque $\vec{\tau}$ acting on a current loop in a magnetic field is given by the formula $\vec{\tau} = \vec{m} \times \vec{B}$, where $\vec{m}$ is the magnetic dipole moment and $\vec{B}$ is the magnetic field induction.

The magnitude of the torque is given by $\tau = mB \sin \theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the area vector $\vec{A}$ (which is perpendicular to the plane of the loop) and the magnetic field vector $\vec{B}$.

The problem states that the plane of the loop is perpendicular to the magnetic field. This implies that the area vector $\vec{A}$ is parallel to the magnetic field vector $\vec{B}$.

Therefore, the angle $\theta$ between the area vector and the magnetic field is $0^{{}^{\circ}}$.

Substituting this into the torque formula: $\tau = mB \sin(0^{{}^{\circ}}) = mB \times 0 = 0$.

Thus, the torque acting on the circular loop is zero.

Answer: zero

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A magnetic field does not interact with:
questions.solution:
The magnetic force $\vec{F}$ on a charge $q$ moving with velocity $\vec{v}$ in a magnetic field $\vec{B}$ is given by the Lorentz force law: $\vec{F} = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$.

If the electric charge is at rest, its velocity $\vec{v} = 0$.

Substituting $\vec{v} = 0$ into the force equation, we get $\vec{F} = q(0 \times \vec{B}) = 0$.

Therefore, a magnetic field exerts no force on an electric charge at rest.

Answer: An electric charge at rest.

questions.q: A square wire of each side l carries a current $I$. The magnetic field at the mid-point of the square
questions.solution:
Magnetic field due to a finite wire at perpendicular distance $d$ is $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi d}(\sin\theta_1 + \sin\theta_2)$, where $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ are angles subtended by the ends of the wire at the point.

For the center of the square, perpendicular distance from center to each side is $d = \dfrac{l}{2}$, and $\theta_1 = \theta_2 = 45°$.

Field due to one side:

$B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi \cdot \dfrac{l}{2}}(\sin 45° + \sin 45°) = \dfrac{2\mu_0 I}{4\pi l} \cdot \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{2}} = 2\sqrt{2}\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I}{l}$

By right-hand rule, all four sides produce field in the same direction at the center.

$B_{total} = 4 \times B_1 = 8\sqrt{2}\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I}{l}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two very long straight parallel wires carry currents $i$ and $2 i$ in opposite directions. The distance between the wires is $r$. At a certain instant of time a point charge $q$ is at. a point equidistant from the two wires in the plane of the wires. Its instantaneous velocity $v$ is perpendicular to this plane. The magnitude of the force due to the magnetic field acting on the charge at this instant is
questions.solution:
Let the two wires be placed along the $y$-axis at $x = -r/2$ and $x = r/2$. The wire at $x = -r/2$ carries current $i$ in the $+y$ direction, and the wire at $x = r/2$ carries current $2i$ in the $-y$ direction.

The point charge $q$ is at the origin $(0,0,0)$ and its velocity is $\vec{v} = v \hat{k}$.

The magnetic field $\vec{B}_1$ due to the first wire at the origin is given by the right-hand rule. The distance is $r/2$. The field is $\vec{B}_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 i}{2 \pi (r/2)} \hat{k} = \dfrac{\mu_0 i}{\pi r} \hat{k}$.

The magnetic field $\vec{B}_2$ due to the second wire at the origin. The current is $2i$ in the $-y$ direction. The distance is $r/2$. The field is $\vec{B}_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 (2i)}{2 \pi (r/2)} \hat{k} = \dfrac{2 \mu_0 i}{\pi r} \hat{k}$.

The total magnetic field at the origin is $\vec{B} = \vec{B}_1 + \vec{B}_2 = \left( \dfrac{\mu_0 i}{\pi r} + \dfrac{2 \mu_0 i}{\pi r} \right) \hat{k} = \dfrac{3 \mu_0 i}{\pi r} \hat{k}$.

The magnetic force on the charge is $\vec{F} = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$. Since $\vec{v} = v \hat{k}$ and $\vec{B} = B \hat{k}$, the cross product $\hat{k} \times \hat{k} = 0$.

Therefore, the magnetic force acting on the charge is zero.

Answer: zero

questions.q: A straight wire of length $2 \mathrm{ m}$ carries a current of $10 \mathrm{ A}$. If this wire is placed in uniform magnetic field of $0.15 \mathrm{ T}$ making an angle of $45^{{}^{\circ}}$ with the magnetic field, the applied force on the wire will be
questions.solution:
The force $F$ on a current-carrying wire of length $L$ in a uniform magnetic field $B$ is given by the formula $F = I L B \sin(\theta)$, where $I$ is the current and $\theta$ is the angle between the wire and the magnetic field.

Given values are:
$I = 10 \text{ A}$
$L = 2 \text{ m}$
$B = 0.15 \text{ T}$
$\theta = 45^{{}^{\circ}}$

Substituting these values into the formula:
$F = 10 \times 2 \times 0.15 \times \sin(45^{{}^{\circ}})$

$F = 20 \times 0.15 \times \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

$F = 3 \times \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}} \text{ N}$

Answer: $3 / \sqrt{2} \mathrm{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An electric current $I$ enters and leaves a uniform circular wire of radius $r$ through diametrically opposite points. A charged particle $q$ moves along the axis of circular wire passes through its centre with speed $v$. The magnetic force on the particle when it passes through the centre has a magnitude
questions.solution:
The circular wire is divided into two semi-circular segments by the diametrically opposite points where the current enters and leaves. Let the current $I$ split into $I_1$ and $I_2$ through the two semi-circular paths. Since the wire is uniform, the resistance of each semi-circular path is equal, so $I_1 = I_2 = I/2$.

The magnetic field $B_1$ at the center due to the first semi-circular wire carrying current $I/2$ is directed perpendicular to the plane of the loop. Using the Biot-Savart law, the magnetic field at the center of a full circular loop is $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2r}$. For a semi-circular wire, the field is half of this, $B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 (I/2)}{4r} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{8r}$.

The magnetic field $B_2$ at the center due to the second semi-circular wire carrying current $I/2$ is also $\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{8r}$, but its direction is opposite to that of $B_1$ because the current flows in the opposite sense relative to the center. Thus, the net magnetic field $B_{net} = B_1 - B_2 = 0$.

The magnetic force on a charged particle moving with velocity $v$ is given by $\vec{F} = q(\vec{v} imes \vec{B})$. Since the net magnetic field $\vec{B}$ at the center is zero, the magnetic force on the particle is $F = q v (0) = 0$.

Answer: 0

questions.solution:
The magnetic moment $\vec{\mu}$ of a planar current loop is given by $\mu = N I A$, where $N$ is the number of turns, $I$ is the current, and $A$ is the area of the loop.

The total length of the wire is $L = 24m$. The perimeter of a regular hexagon with side length $m$ is $P = 6m$.

The number of turns $N$ is the total length of the wire divided by the perimeter of one hexagon:
$N = \dfrac{L}{P} = \dfrac{24m}{6m} = 4$.

The area $A$ of a regular hexagon with side length $m$ is given by:
$A = \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2} m^2$.

Substituting these values into the formula for magnetic moment:
$\mu = N I A = 4 \times I \times \left( \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2} m^2 \right)$
$\mu = 2 \times 3\sqrt{3} I m^2 = 6\sqrt{3} I m^2$.

questions.q: Two particles of masses $m_{1}=m, m_{2}=2 m$ and charges $q_{1}=q, q_{2}=2 q$ entered into uniform magnetic field with the same velocity and at the same angle. Find $F_{1} / F_{2}$ (force ratio).
questions.solution:
The magnetic force acting on a charged particle moving in a uniform magnetic field is given by the expression $\vec{F} = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$.

The magnitude of the force is $F = qvB \sin \theta$, where $v$ is the velocity of the particle, $B$ is the magnetic field strength, and $\theta$ is the angle between the velocity vector and the magnetic field vector.

The particles enter the magnetic field with the same velocity $v$ and at the same angle $\theta$ relative to the magnetic field, the force on each particle is $F_1 = q_1 v B \sin \theta$ and $F_2 = q_2 v B \sin \theta$.

Substituting the given values $q_1 = q$ and $q_2 = 2q$, we get $F_1 = qvB \sin \theta$ and $F_2 = 2qvB \sin \theta$.

The ratio of the forces is $\dfrac{F_1}{F_2} = \dfrac{qvB \sin \theta}{2qvB \sin \theta} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{2}$

$n = 20 \text{ turns cm}^{-1} = 20 \times 10^{2} \text{ turns m}^{-1} = 2000 \text{ m}^{-1}$
$\mu_{0} = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \text{ T m A}^{-1}$

Substituting these values into the formula:
$20 \times 10^{-3} = (4\pi \times 10^{-7}) \times (2000) \times I$

$20 \times 10^{-3} = 8\pi \times 10^{-4} \times I$

$I = \dfrac{20 \times 10^{-3}}{8\pi \times 10^{-4}} = \dfrac{200}{8\pi} = \dfrac{25}{\pi}$

Using $\pi \approx 3.14$:
$I \approx \dfrac{25}{3.14} \approx 7.96 \text{ A}$

Rounding to the nearest integer, we get $I \approx 8 \text{ A}$.

Answer: $8 \mathrm{ A}$
